problem: Most social navigation work learns or hand-codes only the local controller, which leaves the robot open to local minima and ignores the social quality of the global path. Hand-crafted models such as the Social Force Model do not adapt well, IRL assumes known or linear reward features, and GAN-based imitation needs a lot of data. Purely learned controllers also fail unpredictably when they have to extrapolate outside the training distribution.
motivation: Robots sharing space with people need navigation that humans find comfortable and legible, not just collision-free. Conditional Neural Processes can encode complex, multimodal trajectory distributions from relatively few demonstrations. This makes them a candidate for learning socially compliant behaviour at both the global and the local planning layers. Because any learned controller breaks down on out-of-range inputs, a safety arbitration mechanism is also needed.
key_idea: A hierarchical navigation stack uses CNPs trained on demonstrations for both the global trajectory generator and the local velocity controller. A Random Network Distillation (or GAN) out-of-distribution detector hands control to a Social Force Model fallback whenever the learned controllers would have to extrapolate.
insight: The CNP averages latent encodings of conditioning observations. This lets it keep several demonstration modes, such as passing a pedestrian on the left or on the right. A plain 5-layer FFNN instead regresses to the mean of those modes and produces paths that cut close to pedestrians. Over 1000 random environments the CNP global controller had larger closest distances and fewer and shorter proxemic-zone intrusions than the FFNN, and the difference was statistically significant under t- and z-tests at 0.95. Learned controllers still extrapolate badly: without the Failure Prediction Module, 14 of 50 cluttered tests ended in collisions. RND-based OOD detection with an SFM fallback removes these collisions, at the cost of more zone intrusions, and RND was found more stable than a GAN discriminator. A data-scale ablation shows the local CNP needs at least 500 demonstrations to avoid collisions; at D=1500 it reaches zero intimate and personal zone intrusions.
method: Data-Driven Global Controller (CNP): the input is time t, the task parameter is the scene configuration (start, goal, pedestrian positions) and the output is the 2D position. MLP encoder latents of n≤10 sampled observations are averaged, and a query network outputs a bivariate Gaussian (μ, Σ) at any query time. It is trained by negative log-likelihood and queried at all time steps in parallel to produce a full trajectory, from which via-points are sampled uniformly.

Data-Driven Local Controller (CNP): the input X is the relative position of the current via-point, the task parameter γ(X) is the relative pedestrian position(s) and the output is a Gaussian over the 2D base velocity (vx, vy). It uses up to 20 observations, a 256-384-512 encoder and a 512-384-256 query network. At test time only the closest pedestrian is fed in, and it runs in real time.

Failure Prediction Module: an OOD detector trained on the same demonstration states. Option 1 is a standard GAN whose discriminator probability scores in-distribution-ness (more stable than W-GAN here). Option 2, preferred, is Random Network Distillation: a fixed random 3x512 MLP target and a trained predictor, where a high prediction error flags extrapolation.

Hand-Crafted Reactive Controller: a Social Force Model fallback that takes over while the state is out of distribution. Control returns to the CNP local controller once the Failure Prediction Module judges the state in-range again. The architecture is subsumption-inspired.
Replanning: if the local controller fails to follow the path (e.g., a pedestrian blocks it), the global CNP is re-queried to produce a new trajectory for the same task.

Demonstration data: 1500 simulated trajectories generated by an SFM-controlled robot with random start, goal and pedestrian placements. A second variant uses 30 manually annotated pedestrian-encounter clips from SCAND (real-world teleoperation), interpolated, converted to egocentric frame and augmented by rotation.

setting.backbone: Conditional Neural Processes (MLP encoder + query network) for global and local controllers, plus an RND/GAN OOD detector, trained from scratch; Social Force Model fallback
setting.training_data: 1500 SFM-generated demonstration trajectories in CoppeliaSim with random start, goal and single/multiple, static/dynamic pedestrians. Alternative local-controller variant: 30 manually extracted and annotated pedestrian-encounter scenarios from SCAND (real-world teleoperated robot), interpolated, egocentric and rotation-augmented. The same data trains the GAN/RND detectors.
setting.observation: high-level state vectors: relative goal/via-point position and relative positions of pedestrians (closest pedestrian at test time); global controller receives start, goal and pedestrian positions
setting.action_space: continuous 2D base velocity (vx, vy) for an omnidirectional robot; global controller outputs a continuous 2D trajectory sampled into via-points
setting.privileged: ground-truth pedestrian positions and robot/goal relative positions from the simulator (no perception pipeline); pedestrian positions known to the global planner

numbers_note: Not a standard embodied-navigation benchmark; all tests are custom CoppeliaSim scenarios, and metrics are social-navigation ones (ADE, PL, ATG, AA, proxemic zone intrusion counts). Several key results appear only as bar plots without printed numbers: global CNP vs FFNN over 1000 random environments (closest distance, zone intrusion counts and durations), the full pipeline vs A* + Elastic Bands, and the with/without Failure Prediction Module (GAN vs RND) ablation over 50 tests. The only numbers stated in text for that ablation are: extrapolation errors occurred in 14 of 50 tests and led to collisions without the FPM. Std values (±) in the tables are reported only in the evidence fields.
results: In 25 simulated tests, the local CNP trained on SFM-generated simulation data had ADE 0.53, path length 13.49 and 0 personal-zone intrusions. These are comparable to the SFM expert it imitates (ADE 0.43, PL 13.18, PZIC 0), not better. The SCAND-trained variant is much slower (ATG 69.86 vs 34.83) and has 3 personal-zone intrusions. According to figure-only results, the CNP global controller keeps larger distances and makes fewer and shorter proxemic intrusions than an FFNN over 1000 random scenes, and the full pipeline beats A* + Elastic Bands on the same metrics (t-test, 0.95). Without the Failure Prediction Module, 14 of 50 cluttered tests ended in collisions. With the RND/GAN detector plus SFM fallback these were caught (RND once too late), though zone intrusions increased. The local controller becomes collision-free only with at least 500 demonstrations.
limitations: Simulation only, with simulated pedestrians. The expert demonstrations come from the SFM itself, so the learned controller mostly reproduces SFM and does not outperform it; no standard benchmark or strong learned baselines are used.
Relies on ground-truth high-level inputs (relative pedestrian/goal positions), ignores pedestrian orientation and velocity, and the local controller only considers the closest pedestrian.
The global controller loses timing information because demonstrations are interpolated. Many results are reported only as figures, with a small test set (25 or 50 environments).
compares_to: pipeline without Failure Prediction Module (GAN vs RND detector)
